To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GTP and GTP[γ‐S] stimulate and GDP[β S ] inhibits the adenylate cyclases of E. coli and that glucose inhibits this enzyme in an uncompetitive manner.

the adenylate cyclases of E. coli and of other bacteria have a regulatory domain which is similar to the regulatory domain of the mammalian enzyme and which is activated in a dose-dependent manner by GTP.
GDP[βS]-inhibited adenylate cyclases are activated by GTP and that the inhibition is partially relieved by GTP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of glucose and nucleotides on E. coli adenylate cyclases, and with their possible physiological significance.
the regulation of bacterial adenylate cyclases by nucleotides, particularly the GTP‐binding proteins.
the effects of glucose and of GTP and its analogues on adenylate activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

GDP[βS]: (1) is a potent inhibitor of adenylate‐cyclase activity in intact E. coli ; (2) does not act as a competitive inhibitor of GTP; (3) inhibits adenylate‐ cyclase activity in a dose‐related manner; (4) is not a substrate for adenylate cyclases in intact E. col i.

GDP[βS]: (i) is a competitive antagonist at the guanine‐nucleotide site; (ii) inhibits adenylate cyclases by an allosteric mechanism; (iii) is not a substrate for adenylate cyclas; and (iv) is not an inhibitor of phosphodiesterase.
GDP[βS]-inhibited E.coli adenlyate cyclase was not activated by GTP, but that GTP‐activated E. coli adenylate cyclse was partially inhibited by GDP[βS].
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GDP[βS]. a non‐phophorylatable analogue of GTP, inhibits adenylate cyclases from both eukaryotes and prokaryotes, and that glucose inhibits the E. coli adenylate cyclas.
the adenylate cyclases of both prokaryotes and eukaryotes are inhibited by GDP, and activated by GTP, but that the effects of GDP[βS ] and GTP[γ S ] on the enzyme are species‐ and tissue‐specific.

the effects of GDP[βS]/GTP on E. coli adenylate cyclases are similar to those observed with mammalian systems, and the effects of glucose on E. coli are similar to the effects of glucose in the liver of the rat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of GTP[γ‐S] and GDP[β‐S] as analogs of GTP and GDP is not justified, because they are not analogs of GMP.
the use of GDP[βS](a nonhydrolyzable analog of GDP) as an experimental tool to study G protein‐mediated signaling is problematic.
